elements.quote: A previous systematic review of the literature describing studies conducted in the Caribbean that presented the distribution of diabetes, its outcomes, and risk factors, by one or more social determinants, was updated
elements.reason: The abstract explicitly identifies the report as an updated systematic review.

elements.quote: Objectives. To conduct an analysis of the most recent data on diabetes and its risk factors by gender and other social determinants of health to understand why its prevalence is higher among women than men in the Caribbean; to inform policy agenda-setting for diabetes prevention and control in the Caribbean; and to identify gaps in the evidence that require further research.
elements.reason: The abstract clearly states the objectives of the review.

elements.quote: A previous systematic review of the literature describing studies conducted in the Caribbean that presented the distribution of diabetes, its outcomes, and risk factors, by one or more social determinants, was updated to include sources from 1 January 2007 - 31 December 2016.
elements.reason: The abstract specifies the inclusion criteria regarding the topic (diabetes, outcomes, risk factors, social determinants), population (Caribbean), and date range.

elements.quote: Surveys by the World Health Organization (WHO) were also included.
elements.reason: The abstract mentions WHO surveys but fails to identify the primary bibliographic information sources (e.g., PubMed, EMBASE) used to identify studies, nor does it report when the search was last performed.
The abstract does not describe the methods used to assess the risk of bias in the included studies.

elements.quote: Where data were sufficient, meta-analyses were undertaken.
elements.reason: The abstract specifies that meta-analyses were used to synthesize the results.

elements.quote: A total of 8 326 manuscripts were identified. Of those, 282 were selected for full text review, and 114, for abstraction. In all, 36 papers, including WHO-related surveys, had sufficient information for meta-analysis.
elements.reason: The abstract reports the number of studies identified and included.

elements.quote: More women compared to men were obese (OR: 2.1; 95%CI = 1.65 - 2.69), physically inactive (OR: 2.18; 95%CI = 1.75 - 2.72), and had diabetes (OR: 1.48; 95%CI = 1.25 - 1.76). More men smoked (OR: 4.27; 95%CI = 3.18 - 5.74) and had inadequate fruit and vegetable intake (OR: 1.37; 95%CI = 1.21 - 1.57)
elements.reason: The abstract presents the main results for the outcomes.

elements.quote: Diabetes is a major cause of death and disability around the world and is projected to increase in the coming decades (1). Type 2 diabetes represents 80% - 90% of the total diabetes burden, with the main proximal risk factors being overweight and obesity, physical inactivity, unhealthy diet, and tobacco smoking (1). The prevalence of type 2 diabetes and its risk factors are strongly associated with underlying social and economic factors (2), with poorer, less educated people often being disproportionally affected.
elements.reason: The manuscript describes the current state of knowledge regarding diabetes, its risk factors, and their association with social and economic factors.

elements.quote: The objective of this review was to inform policy agenda-setting for diabetes prevention and control in the Caribbean, and to identify gaps in the evidence where further research is needed.
elements.reason: The manuscript explicitly states the objective of the review, which serves as the rationale for conducting it (to inform policy and identify evidence gaps).

elements.quote: Sobers-Grannum and colleagues examined the effects of gender on diabetes, its risk factors, and outcomes in the Caribbean in a systematic review published in 2015 (4). In addition to gender, the review sought to describe data on a range of social determinants of health, but evidence was scant... Guided by the analytical framework recommended by the WHO Commission on the Social Determinants of Health (3), the present study updates the previous systematic review (4) with new data
elements.reason: The manuscript identifies a previous systematic review (Sobers-Grannum et al., 2015) and explains that the current review is an update to include new data and a wider range of social determinants.
This is a systematic review of observational studies on social determinants of diabetes, not a review of intervention effects; therefore, a proposed mechanism of action is not required.
The review is not focused on evaluating complex interventions or delivery contexts, so a logic model is not required.

elements.quote: The objective of this review was to inform policy agenda-setting for diabetes prevention and control in the Caribbean, and to identify gaps in the evidence where further research is needed.
elements.reason: The review explicitly states its objectives in the text, defining the scope (diabetes and risk factors in the Caribbean) and the purpose (policy agenda-setting and identifying research gaps).

This is an observational systematic review examining the social determinants of diabetes and related risk factors, not a review of intervention effects; therefore, the requirement to state planned comparisons using PICO does not apply.

elements.quote: Caribbean study population Adult participants ( ≥ 18 years of age) when considering diabetes and its outcomes, or participants ≥ 12 years when considering risk factors Outcomes stratified by at least one of the social determinants Quantitative study design (observational/intervention) Risk of bias was assessed using criteria applied by Brown and colleagues (14) for each relationship and classified as follows: Sample size ≥ 50 people
elements.reason: The manuscript specifies the study population (Caribbean, age requirements), study design (quantitative observational/intervention), and sample size requirements.
